questions.question: In a high-dimensional feature space, why is cosine similarity often preferred over raw inner products when comparing neuron activations?
questions.choice_A: Cosine similarity removes the effect of vector magnitude, highlighting directional alignment
questions.choice_B: Cosine similarity always yields a value larger than the inner product
questions.choice_C: Cosine similarity is differentiable while inner products are not
questions.choice_D: Cosine similarity equals the Euclidean distance when vectors are normalized

questions.question: Viewing a neuron as a weight vector in $\mathbb{R}^d$, what is the geometric meaning of the neuron's pre-activation $z = w^\top x$?
questions.choice_A: The squared Euclidean distance between $w$ and $x$
questions.choice_B: The projection of $x$ onto $w$ scaled by $\|w\|_2$
questions.choice_C: The angle between $w$ and $x$ measured in radians
questions.choice_D: The cosine similarity between $w$ and $x$ scaled by $\|x\|_2$ only

questions.question: What is a primary consequence of constraining weight vectors to unit norm (e.g., weight normalization or explicit re-normalization)?
questions.choice_A: It guarantees orthogonality among different neurons
questions.choice_B: It prevents overfitting by eliminating bias terms
questions.choice_C: It decouples the neuron's direction from its scale, making activations depend purely on angle with inputs
questions.choice_D: It makes the network invariant to input scaling

questions.question: Two filters have identical cosine similarity with a set of inputs but different $\ell_2$ norms. Which outcome is most likely if the model uses raw dot products for scoring?
questions.choice_A: They will induce identical decision boundaries
questions.choice_B: The filter with smaller norm will produce larger pre-activations
questions.choice_C: Both filters will be orthogonal to all inputs
questions.choice_D: The filter with larger norm will produce larger-magnitude pre-activations on average

questions.question: Which statement best captures the geometric meaning of the angle between two vectors $u$ and $v$ in $\mathbb{R}^d$?
questions.choice_A: It is defined by $\cos \theta = \frac{u^\top v}{\|u\|_2\,\|v\|_2}$ and measures directional alignment independent of scale
questions.choice_B: It equals $\|u-v\|_2$ and measures how far apart the vectors are
questions.choice_C: It is zero unless the vectors are orthonormal
questions.choice_D: It depends only on the norms of $u$ and $v$

questions.question: In a linear classifier $f(x)=\operatorname{sign}(w^\top x + b)$, how does scaling $w$ and $b$ by a positive constant $\alpha$ affect the decision boundary?
questions.choice_A: It rotates the hyperplane
questions.choice_B: It leaves the hyperplane unchanged
questions.choice_C: It translates the hyperplane without rotation
questions.choice_D: It makes the classifier nonlinear

questions.question: Why can unit-norm constraints on weights improve interpretability of learned features?
questions.choice_A: They enforce sparsity in the weight vectors
questions.choice_B: They align all neurons to be mutually orthogonal
questions.choice_C: They normalize away magnitude, allowing comparison of neuron directions as features
questions.choice_D: They linearize the loss landscape

questions.question: If inputs are normalized to unit norm but weights are not, what quantity does the pre-activation $w^\top x$ primarily reflect?
questions.choice_A: Only the angle between $w$ and $x$
questions.choice_B: Only the norm of $x$
questions.choice_C: A combination of the angle and the norm of $w$
questions.choice_D: Only the bias term

questions.question: What does orthogonality of two neuron weight vectors imply in terms of their responses to typical inputs?
questions.choice_A: They will always produce identical activations on all inputs
questions.choice_B: They capture statistically independent features
questions.choice_C: They are uncorrelated with respect to the standard inner product
questions.choice_D: They have equal norms

questions.question: Which statement best contrasts cosine similarity and Euclidean distance for comparing feature vectors in high dimensions?
questions.choice_A: Cosine similarity is sensitive to magnitude while Euclidean distance is not
questions.choice_B: Both are invariant to uniform rescaling of vectors
questions.choice_C: Euclidean distance mixes magnitude and direction, while cosine focuses on direction
questions.choice_D: Euclidean distance is always smaller in high dimensions

questions.question: Consider a linear layer $y = Wx$. If each row of $W$ is re-scaled by a positive scalar specific to that row, what changes and what remains the same for the layer's geometry?
questions.choice_A: The orientation of each hyperplane changes, but margins stay the same
questions.choice_B: The orientation of each hyperplane stays the same, but distances to the hyperplanes are re-scaled
questions.choice_C: Both orientation and location of hyperplanes are unchanged
questions.choice_D: The layer becomes nonlinear

questions.question: Why does batch normalization often make networks less sensitive to the scale of weights and inputs?
questions.choice_A: It enforces exact unit-norm weights
questions.choice_B: It replaces inner products with cosine similarity
questions.choice_C: It standardizes pre-activations, removing mean and scaling variance
questions.choice_D: It fixes the angle between weights and inputs

questions.question: When analyzing learned filters as points on the unit sphere, what does clustering of filters indicate?
questions.choice_A: Multiple filters sharing similar directions and thus similar feature selectivity
questions.choice_B: Filters with identical norms but unrelated directions
questions.choice_C: Orthogonality among filters
questions.choice_D: A failure of the optimization to converge

questions.question: In weight normalization, a weight vector is parameterized as $w = \frac{g}{\|v\|_2} v$. What is the main benefit of this reparameterization?
questions.choice_A: It prevents vanishing gradients by increasing norms automatically
questions.choice_B: It decouples the length (scale) $g$ from the direction $v/\|v\|_2$, aiding optimization
questions.choice_C: It guarantees orthogonality across neurons
questions.choice_D: It ensures invariance to rotations of the input space

questions.question: Suppose two inputs $x_1$ and $x_2$ have the same cosine similarity with a neuron weight $w$, but $\|x_1\|_2 > \|x_2\|_2$. Using raw dot products, how will their pre-activations compare?
questions.choice_A: $w^\top x_1 < w^\top x_2$
questions.choice_B: $w^\top x_1 = w^\top x_2$
questions.choice_C: $w^\top x_1 > w^\top x_2$
questions.choice_D: They are incomparable without knowing $\|w\|_2$

questions.question: What is the geometric interpretation of the bias term $b$ in $w^\top x + b$ for a linear classifier?
questions.choice_A: It rotates the decision hyperplane
questions.choice_B: It scales the distance to the hyperplane
questions.choice_C: It translates the hyperplane along the normal direction $w$
questions.choice_D: It enforces unit-norm for $w$

questions.question: How does enforcing orthonormal rows in a linear layer’s weight matrix $W$ affect the mapping $y=Wx$?
questions.choice_A: It preserves both angles and lengths for all vectors
questions.choice_B: It preserves angles but uniformly scales all lengths by the same constant
questions.choice_C: It preserves lengths but distorts angles
questions.choice_D: It preserves lengths and angles only within the row-span subspace

questions.question: In the context of representation learning, why might maximizing the angle (minimizing cosine similarity) between class prototypes be beneficial?
questions.choice_A: It reduces inter-class directional overlap, promoting larger angular margins
questions.choice_B: It guarantees lower training loss on all batches
questions.choice_C: It ensures prototypes have equal norms
questions.choice_D: It makes Euclidean distances between prototypes independent of scale

questions.question: For two vectors $u$ and $v$, what does $u^\top v = 0$ imply about their cosine similarity and angle?
questions.choice_A: Cosine similarity is 1 and $\theta=0$
questions.choice_B: Cosine similarity is undefined
questions.choice_C: Cosine similarity is 0 and $\theta=\pi/2$
questions.choice_D: Cosine similarity is -1 and $\theta=\pi$

questions.question: Which training pathology can arise from relying only on dot products without normalization, especially when learning rate schedules interact with weight scales?
questions.choice_A: Scale-direction entanglement, where changing weight norms confounds effective step sizes
questions.choice_B: Guaranteed divergence due to non-convexity
questions.choice_C: Loss of differentiability of the model
questions.choice_D: Over-enforcement of orthogonality

questions.question: If a research paper claims a method is "scale-invariant" with respect to features, what is the most precise interpretation?
questions.choice_A: Predictions do not change when inputs are multiplied by any nonzero scalar
questions.choice_B: Gradients are always zero with respect to input scale
questions.choice_C: Training loss is constant across all parameter settings
questions.choice_D: Model weights are constrained to have unit norm
